extracted.intended_audience: students of painting and practising artists (art students/early-career and advanced painters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for painters on how to study, imitate, and borrow from nature, predecessors, and various schools to develop taste, invention, and mastery throughout their careers. Covers what to imitate, what to avoid (servile copying, peculiarities), how to borrow without plagiarising, and the lifelong discipline of study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject the myth of inspiration; art is acquired
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not regard artistic power as a peculiar gift of inspiration given at birth; treat art as an acquireable skill open to study and methodical effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who view art as 'a kind of inspiration' mistake what is in reality the product of long labour and gradual gradation. The untaught mind mistakes complex skill for magic; the practical artist should examine means by which the art may be acquired and strengthened rather than appeal to miraculous gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation is necessary (of nature and other painters)
rubrics_metrics.description: A painter must necessarily be an imitator of the works of nature and of other painters; imitation is foundational to the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This necessity dispels the 'phantom of inspiration'—no man can be an artist on other terms. Imitation of nature is primary, and imitation of masters is equally unavoidable and valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with imitation and continue it throughout life
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is essential in the first stages of the art and may, and should, be extended throughout one’s life without danger of enfeebling the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to the view that imitation must cease once one can 'think for ourselves,' continued study of other masters enriches the artist, produces variety and originality, and does not prevent an original air in works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation produces variety, originality, and genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Originality and invention grow out of imitation; 'even genius, at least what generally is so called, is the child of imitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By being conversant with others' inventions we learn to invent; the mind absorbs and recombines materials from many sources to produce new combinations and excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and apply rules; genius operates from refined principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Many qualities once considered the effect of genius (beauty of form, expression, composition) are now governed by rules and principles discoverable by study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism and practice fix these rules. Genius does not mean absence of rules but working from refined, often tacit, principles that the artist senses and applies; thus study of principles is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habituate the mind to contemplation of excellence (lifelong exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continually expose your mind to great works; this habit disciplines taste and supplies the intellectual materials for invention at every stage of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The works of masters are 'the food of our infancy' and the 'substance which supplies the fullest maturity' of the artist's vigour. Keep a settled intercourse with true examples of grandeur to fertilise the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulate and digest many materials; more materials yield greater invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A mind enriched by an assemblage of ancient and modern ideas will be more fruitful: the greater the collection of carefully digested ideas, the greater the means of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having many materials increases resources for invention; lack of power to use them indicates feebleness of intellect or poor internal organisation of those collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study nature as the ultimate fountain of excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is the inexhaustible source from which the highest beauty of form must be taken; study of nature should aid, not be excluded by, study of masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use study of masters 'in aid and not in exclusion' of nature. Finding the highest beauty in nature requires long deduction and experience; do not neglect direct observation of the natural world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from works themselves rather than from precepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is better learnt by close study of the works themselves than by merely reading precepts formed upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe how masters achieve effects in practice rather than depending solely on written rules; the works disclose principles that precepts may obscure or fail to capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze underlying devices (composition, light, colour, harmony)
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying a master, enter into contrivance and examine compositional devices: disposition of masses of light, means by which effects are produced, how parts are lost or relieved, and colour harmonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not admire harmony of colouring alone—inspect what colours compose tints and how they act as foils to neighbours. Seizing this 'clue' allows advancement in principle and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose many and proper models; avoid slavish single-master imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confine imitation to one favourite master; take many models and not one sole guide, otherwise the imitator will remain behind and servile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Raphaelle, Poussin, Rembrandt, etc.) show effects of limited imitation. Raffaelle himself imitated multiple masters and antiquity; to equal him one should study widely rather than slavishly follow any single living master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat peculiarities (a manner) as defects to avoid copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiar marks or mannerisms of an individual artist are generally defects and should not be imitated as they become blemishes in the copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peculiarities may escape blame by novelty but when copied they become ridiculous. Even celebrated artists have mannerisms that are faults; the imitator should avoid importing these into his own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select and separate what to imitate within models carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires circumspection to distinguish in a model what should be imitated and what should be rejected; select principles rather than superficial peculiarities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sagacious imitator notes distinguishing features of each master and separates method from mannerism. Focus on contrivance, colour composition, and the means that produce effects rather than prominent but defective marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowing vs plagiarism: borrow openly and improve the idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing a thought, attitude, or figure is warrantable when accommodated and improved so there is no seam; otherwise it may be plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient works are a public magazine of materials and may be copied without shame; from moderns, accomodate and improve the borrowed idea so it becomes part of your work. The artist should 'enter into a competition with his original' and endeavour to improve what he appropriates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use works of antiquity as foundational material (acceptable to copy from ancients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventions and thoughts of the ancients are a common property and a necessary source; trace art to antiquity and study statues, reliefs, coins, and other remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting thoughts of antiquity (e.g., Raphael's collection) supplies a rich store; engraving makes these inventions more accessible. When such materials are used skillfully, they are considered part of one's own possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from inferior artists by extracting their useful elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Even very finished artists in inferior branches and lower schools contain materials worthy of attention which a skilful painter can convert into valuable ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify ingenious compositions, peculiar expressions, mechanical excellences, and modes of telling stories in lesser artists; transform 'from dunghills' into 'pure gold' by passing their hints through your own mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid complacency and continual reliance on one’s former work
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make your earlier works or inferior patterns the standard for later ones; avoid pride and the habit of flattering yourself with narrow standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Academy aims to avoid producing narrow habits. If you choose inferior patterns or let your own former works be the pattern for later work, the fault lies with you; continual external study is necessary to progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise continuous critical judgement; be your own teacher
rubrics_metrics.description: As you advance, form your own standards by criticising, comparing, and ranking masters; study with judgement and suspicion that even great men have faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You are to be your own teacher: retain the practice of studying masters but judge their works against a personal standard formed by continued exposure to excellence. The masters taught you to make that standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the mind fertilised; more knowledge strengthens genius rather than smothers it
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no danger that adding other men's thoughts will smother genius; rather, acquired images act like embers that strengthen a spark of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If another's thoughts encumber you, it indicates lack of native strength. Use acquisitions to consolidate and fashion your own weaker ideas into more finished principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persist in study or risk regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Neglecting to look beyond oneself through study, whether from indolence, vanity, or other reasons, leads to stagnation or decline in artistic performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who stop studying do not merely cease to progress; they often go backward, like men living on capital until reduced to beggary. Continuous study is recommended to avoid such decline.
